questions.q: What does CAST(value AS newType) do?
options: Converts value to newType, using ANSI-standard syntax
Renames a column
Deletes rows of the wrong type
Only works on numeric values
questions.explain: CAST is the standard, portable way to convert between data types.

questions.q: What is the argument order for CONVERT, and how does it differ from CAST?
options: CONVERT(newType, value) — type comes first, reversed compared to CAST(value AS newType)
CONVERT and CAST use the identical argument order
CONVERT takes only one argument
CONVERT(value, newType) — same order as CAST
questions.explain: This reversed order is a common source of confusion when switching between the two functions.

questions.q: What can CONVERT do that CAST cannot?
options: Accept an optional third argument (a style code) to control formatting, especially for dates
Convert text to numbers, which CAST cannot do at all
Run faster in every case
Work with NULL values, unlike CAST
questions.explain: CONVERT's optional style code (like 101 for mm/dd/yyyy) has no CAST equivalent.

questions.q: What happens when you CAST text that isn't actually numeric to an INT?
options: A runtime conversion error occurs
SQL Server silently returns NULL
SQL Server silently returns 0
The text is truncated to fit
questions.explain: Non-convertible values fail at runtime — this is why validating source data (or using TRY_CAST later) matters.

questions.q: When should you prefer CAST over CONVERT?
options: When you want portable, ANSI-standard syntax and don't need special formatting
Whenever converting dates specifically
CAST should never be used — CONVERT is always superior
Only when working with VARCHAR(MAX) columns
questions.explain: CAST is the better default for straightforward, portable conversions; CONVERT earns its place when formatting control is needed.
